text: Legume-based intercropping and cover cropping increase soil organic carbon by 15-25% over 2-3 years through nitrogen fixation and increased root biomass turnover. This effect is strongest in soils starting below 0.5% SOC.
In semi-arid croplands, soil organic carbon below 0.3% is associated with severely reduced microbial biomass and poor water-holding capacity, compounding drought stress on crops.
Semi-arid regions of South Asia are projected to see increased rainfall variability, with low-rainfall years reducing plant-available water by 20-40% relative to historical baselines.
Agricultural intensification and monoculture cropping are among the top drivers of global biodiversity decline, primarily through habitat homogenization and reduced on-farm plant diversity.

Land cover classified as single-crop agricultural mosaic shows markedly lower structural heterogeneity than mixed-cropping or agroforestry systems, correlating with lower habitat connectivity indices.
Habitat fragmentation index correlates strongly with species richness decline: each 10% increase in fragmentation associates with approximately 8% lower local species richness.
Monoculture cropping systems show 2-4x higher pest outbreak frequency than diversified systems, driving increased pesticide dependency and downstream non-target species harm.
Areas with high pesticide application show 30-45% lower non-target insect abundance, directly impacting pollinator populations and food web stability.
Agroforestry interventions in semi-arid agroforestry trials produced 10-20% increases in soil organic carbon over 3-5 years, alongside measurable reductions in local habitat fragmentation.
Cover crop residue reduces soil evaporation and improves infiltration, increasing soil moisture retention by 10-15% relative to bare or single-crop fields.
Ecosystems with higher species survival rates maintain greater functional redundancy, which buffers them against further environmental shocks such as drought or pest outbreaks.

Land-use change toward homogeneous cropping is a leading contributor to habitat fragmentation globally, with monoculture landscapes showing 2-3x higher fragmentation indices than mixed-use landscapes.
